source.title: Edison: His Life and Inventions
source.attribution: Frank Lewis Dyer and Thomas Commerford Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: A child written off as "addled" can flourish with one teacher who believes in him
cards.body:
Edison had just three months of formal schooling. He sat at the foot of his class, his teacher called him "addled", and he half believed he was a dunce. His mother, a former teacher, took him home and taught him herself. Before he was twelve he had worked through Gibbon, Hume and a dictionary of science with her help, and his father paid him a little for every book he mastered.

The label said more about the classroom than about the boy. If you are a parent, teacher or manager, remember that the right setting can turn a struggling learner into an eager one. And if you were once written off, that verdict need not be final.
cards.quote: With her he found study easy and pleasant.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Boyhood at Port Huron, Michigan ¶4
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you have quietly labelled as slow. What would change if you taught or managed them in a different way this week?

quiz.question: What happened after Edison's teacher called him "addled"?
options: He was sent to a stricter school
His mother taught him at home and he read widely
He gave up books for farm work
His father hired a private tutor
quiz.explanation: His mother, an experienced teacher, educated him at home, and he read serious history and science before he was twelve.

cards.title: Treat what you read as a claim to test, not a fact to swallow
cards.body:
As a boy Edison could not read a statement about how nature worked without wanting to prove it right or wrong. Given an elementary physics book, he tried nearly every experiment in it. He filled the family cellar with about two hundred bottles of chemicals, each labelled "Poison" to keep others away, and checked his reading against what actually happened.

This habit of testing ideas stayed with him all his life. You can borrow it on a small scale. When an article, course or colleague makes a claim you could check, check it. A quick test of your own teaches more, and sticks longer, than a dozen confident sentences.
cards.quote: Edison has said that he never saw a statement in any book as to such things that he did not involuntarily challenge, and wish to demonstrate as either right or wrong.
cards.locator: Chapter II. Edison's Pedigree ¶9
cards.apply_it: Pick one claim you read this week that you could test cheaply, and test it before you repeat it to anyone.

quiz.question: How did young Edison respond to statements in science books?
options: He felt driven to prove them right or wrong by experiment
He ignored them and relied on instinct
He wrote to the authors for explanations
quiz.explanation: He challenged every such statement and tried the experiments himself, an early form of his lifelong method.

cards.title: Even a teenage side business grows when you share the profits with helpers
cards.body:
As a newsboy on the Grand Trunk Railroad, Edison did not just sell papers. Within months he had opened two shops in Port Huron and handed them to other boys, who shared in the profits. He shipped fresh vegetables from Detroit in an empty baggage car, bought butter and berries from farmers along the line, and later put another boy to work on a second train. When one helper proved untrustworthy he simply closed that shop.

The lesson is old but useful: you can only be in one place at a time. Giving others a real stake lets an idea grow beyond your own hours, as long as you pick partners you can trust.
cards.quote: After being on the train for several months, I started two stores in Port Huron--one for periodicals, and the other for vegetables, butter, and berries in the season. These were attended by two boys who shared in the profits.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Boyhood at Port Huron, Michigan ¶10
cards.apply_it: Is there a task you keep doing alone that someone could run for you if they had a share in the result?

quiz.question: How did the young Edison run his two Port Huron stores while working on the train?
options: He hired adult managers on salary
Two boys ran them and shared in the profits
quiz.explanation: He gave two boys a share of the profits to run the stores, an early lesson in delegating with incentives.

cards.title: Spot the demand before it arrives, then find a way to meet it
cards.body:
In April 1862 news of the battle of Shiloh drew huge crowds around the newspaper offices in Detroit. Fifteen-year-old Edison guessed the small towns along his railway line would be just as hungry for news. He traded papers to the station telegraph operator to wire the headlines ahead, then walked into the Detroit Free Press and asked for credit on a thousand copies. Crowds were waiting at every stop. He raised his price as he went and sold out.

The idea still works. Notice what people will want before they ask, use whatever tools you have to reach them, and do not let a lack of cash stop you asking for credit.
cards.quote: I decided that instead of the usual one hundred papers I could sell one thousand; but not having sufficient money to purchase that number, I determined in my desperation to see the editor himself and get credit.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Boyhood at Port Huron, Michigan ¶15
cards.apply_it: What is one need your customers or colleagues will have next month? Write down one step you could take today to be ready for it.

quiz.question: How did Edison create demand for his papers on the day of the Shiloh news?
options: He cut his prices in half
He hired extra newsboys in each town
He had the headlines telegraphed ahead to every station
He printed his own special edition
quiz.explanation: He arranged for the news to be wired ahead and posted at each station, so buyers were waiting when his train arrived.

cards.title: Look for what a limitation makes possible, not only what it takes away
cards.body:
Edison grew partly deaf as a teenager, after an incident on the train. Instead of treating it only as a loss, he listed the ways it helped him. In a noisy telegraph office he heard only his own instrument. Because he could not hear weak telephones well, he improved the transmitter until it was loud enough, and that helped make the telephone commercial. He said the busy street noise of Broadway was as quiet to him as a village.

This is not a call to pretend hardship is good. It is a reminder that a constraint can sharpen your focus or push you towards a better solution. Ask what yours could make possible.
cards.quote: This deafness has been of great advantage to me in various ways.
cards.locator: Chapter III. Boyhood at Port Huron, Michigan ¶17
cards.apply_it: Name one limitation you live with. Write down one way it has pushed you to work differently or better.

quiz.question: How did Edison say his deafness helped his work on the telephone?
options: It let him sleep through noisy nights
He had to improve the transmitter until he could hear it, which made the telephone practical
It made him rely on written reports
It meant he never had to answer calls
quiz.explanation: Because he struggled to hear weak signals, he pushed the transmitter to be louder, which made the telephone commercially usable.

cards.title: Move up a skill level by volunteering for the hard work others avoid
cards.body:
In Cincinnati Edison was rated a "plug", an inferior operator. He wanted to be first-class, so he went to the office at night to take down the fast press reports, standing in for anyone who wanted a few hours off, which often meant all night. One night most of the staff were away and the Cleveland press wire needed someone. Edison took it alone until three in the morning. The next day the stern manager glanced at his copy and promoted him to the Louisville night wire at a much higher salary.

Skill grows fastest at the edge of your ability. Volunteering for the demanding work is practice and an audition at the same time.
cards.quote: but he was determined to lift himself into the class of first-class operators
cards.locator: Chapter V. Arduous Years in the Central West ¶10
cards.apply_it: Which demanding task at work or in your craft could you volunteer for this month to stretch your skill?

quiz.question: How did Edison move from a "plug" rating to first-class operator?
options: He practised on demanding night press work and handled it when needed
He invented a faster telegraph key
quiz.explanation: Regular night practice on fast press copy prepared him, and handling the press wire alone earned the promotion.

cards.title: Study the machine while you wait, and you will be ready when it breaks
cards.body:
Edison arrived in New York in 1869 nearly broke and slept in the battery room of a gold-price reporting company while waiting for a job. He used the time to study its complicated transmitter. On his third day the machine crashed, hundreds of messenger boys swarmed in, and the man in charge panicked. Edison had already worked out where the trouble was likely to be. He found a broken spring, fixed it, and within days the owner put him in charge of the whole plant at $300 a month.

Luck tends to find people who have done the homework. Idle time spent understanding the systems around you is rarely wasted.
cards.quote: I went to the indicator, and, having studied it thoroughly, knew where the trouble ought to be, and found it.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Stock Ticker ¶6
cards.apply_it: Pick one tool or system you rely on but do not understand. Spend twenty minutes this week learning how it works.

quiz.question: Why was Edison able to fix the gold indicator when it broke down?
options: The manager told him what to do
He had studied it thoroughly while waiting for work
quiz.explanation: He had used his waiting days to study the machine, so he knew where to look when it failed.

cards.title: Before you build it, make sure someone actually wants it
cards.body:
Edison's first patent was an electric vote recorder that could count a vote in Congress in a minute. He took it to Washington and showed it to a committee. The chairman admired how well it worked, then told him it was the last thing they wanted, because slow roll calls let the minority delay bad laws.

The machine worked perfectly and was useless. Edison drew a lasting lesson from it and decided to invent only things people genuinely needed. Today we would call it checking for demand before building. Talk to the people who will use your idea, and ask what problem it solves for them, before you invest months in it.
cards.quote: Edison determined from that time forth to devote his inventive faculties only to things for which there was a real, genuine demand, something that subserved the actual necessities of humanity.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. Work and Invention in Boston ¶4
cards.apply_it: Before starting your next project, ask three likely users what problem they would want it to solve.

quiz.question: Why did Congress reject Edison's vote recorder?
options: Members did not want faster voting, because delay was a useful tactic
Someone else had patented it first
quiz.explanation: It worked well, but slow roll calls served a purpose for legislators, so there was no demand for it.

cards.title: Price your work by its value to others, not by the hours it cost you
cards.body:
When the president of the Gold and Stock Telegraph Company asked Edison what his ticker inventions were worth, Edison had $5000 in mind and would have settled for $3000. Losing his nerve, he asked for an offer instead. The general offered $40,000. Edison nearly fainted, signed without reading, and later admitted he had judged value by his own time and trouble.

Many people still price this way, by effort rather than by what the work saves or earns for the buyer. Before naming a figure, ask what your work is worth to the person paying. And when you are unsure, letting the other side name a number first can work in your favour.
cards.quote: for at that time I determined the value by the time and trouble, and not by what the invention was worth to others.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. The Stock Ticker ¶12
cards.apply_it: For one piece of work you sell or do, estimate what it saves or earns for the person receiving it.

quiz.question: How had Edison been valuing his inventions before the $40,000 offer?
options: By the time and trouble they cost him
By what they were worth to the buyer
quiz.explanation: He judged by his own effort, not by the value to the company, which was far higher.

cards.title: Most of what looks like genius is hard work, persistence and common sense
cards.body:
Edison disliked being called a genius. His famous line was that genius is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration. When an old associate praised his genius, he brushed it off with "Stuff!" and named three plainer things instead.

His colleagues pushed back, pointing out that he often saw a route nobody else had seen. Both are probably true. Insight matters, but it usually shows up for people who are already deep in the work. If you are waiting to feel inspired before starting, flip the order. Start, keep at it and use your common sense, and the good ideas are more likely to arrive.
cards.quote: Stuff! I tell you genius is hard work, stick-to-it-iveness, and common sense.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶28
cards.apply_it: Choose one project you have been waiting to feel inspired about and put in 25 focused minutes on it today.

quiz.question: What did Edison say genius really consists of?
options: Hard work, stick-to-it-iveness, and common sense
Natural talent and a good education
quiz.explanation: He insisted that what people called genius was mostly sustained effort and practical judgement.

cards.title: A failed attempt is a result: you now know one more thing that won't work
cards.body:
After more than five months of work on a new storage battery, Edison had run over nine thousand experiments without a promising lead. His colleague Walter Mallory said it was a shame to get no results. Edison turned on him, smiling, and corrected him. He had a great many results.

A few weeks later, after more than ten thousand trials, he found the missing link. Seeing every dead end as information keeps you moving when progress feels invisible. When something you try does not work, write down what it ruled out. That list is real progress, even on the days it does not feel like it.
cards.quote: Results! Why, man, I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶53
cards.apply_it: Think of something that has not worked yet. List three things it taught you to rule out.

quiz.question: How did Edison describe nine thousand unsuccessful battery experiments?
options: As proof the battery was impossible
As a lot of results, since he knew thousands of things that would not work
quiz.explanation: He treated each failure as useful knowledge that narrowed the search.

cards.title: Every experiment succeeds if it clears the air for the next one
cards.body:
Edward Acheson, a young assistant at Menlo Park, once ran an experiment that did not give the result he hoped for. He was moaning about the failure when Edison came in. Edison listened and cheerfully told him not to see it that way. Every experiment cleared things up, and even one that missed its goal was a lesson for future work.

Acheson, who later invented carborundum, believed this happy view of experiments was a large part of Edison's success. It is a good outlook for any project. Before you write an attempt off, ask what it showed you about where to look next.
cards.quote: he considered every experiment a success, as in all cases it cleared up the atmosphere
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶40
cards.apply_it: After your next disappointing attempt at something, write one sentence on what it taught you about where to try next.

quiz.question: What did Edison tell Acheson about his "failed" experiment?
options: To repeat it exactly until it worked
That every experiment is a success because it clears things up for future work
quiz.explanation: Edison saw even a failed experiment as useful, because it narrowed down the problem.

cards.title: Be suspicious of your own success until you can repeat it
cards.body:
Edison expected only about one experiment in a hundred to succeed, and even that one he distrusted until it worked again and again. When his first phonograph played back "Mary had a little lamb" on the very first try, he said he had never been so taken aback, because he was always afraid of things that worked the first time. Experience had taught him that new things usually hid problems before they were ready for sale.

That healthy suspicion is easy to forget when a result flatters us. Before you celebrate a win, a good test or a promising number, check whether you can get it twice.
cards.quote: Edison has frequently remarked that out of a hundred experiments he does not expect more than one to be successful, and as to that one he is always suspicious until frequent repetition has verified the original results.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶41
cards.apply_it: Take one recent success you are proud of. What would it take to confirm it was not a one-off?

quiz.question: How did Edison treat an experiment that succeeded?
options: He stayed suspicious until repeated trials confirmed it
He assumed his theory was proven
quiz.explanation: He trusted a result only after frequent repetition gave the same outcome.

cards.title: Read everything on the subject, then check it with your own hands
cards.body:
Before starting any line of research, Edison read all he could find on it, sifting what others had done until there was nothing left to learn from print. But he did not take their conclusions as settled. He often repeated published experiments in his own way and got quite different results.

It is a balance worth copying. Reading first saves you from reinventing the wheel. Testing for yourself saves you from inheriting someone else's mistakes. When you take on something new, do the homework, then try the key claims yourself before you build on them.
cards.quote: Not that he takes it for granted that the conclusions are correct, for he frequently obtains vastly different results by repeating in his own way experiments made by others as detailed in books.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶13
cards.apply_it: For a topic you are tackling now, list the three claims your plan depends on most, and test one of them yourself.

quiz.question: What did Edison do with experiments he read about in books?
options: Repeated them his own way, often getting different results
Sent them to others to check
quiz.explanation: He mastered the literature first, then repeated key experiments himself rather than trusting them blindly.

cards.title: A discovery you did not write down is almost as bad as no discovery
cards.body:
Edison kept notebooks everywhere in his laboratory, and by 1910 there were over a thousand of them, full of sketches, ideas and test results. His instructions demanded that every sample be labelled so the experiment could be repeated. He knew the cost of skipping this. One explorer he sent to South America found an excellent bamboo for lamp filaments, then lost track of where it grew.

We all lose good ideas, useful links and fixes that worked because we trusted memory. A simple habit of noting what you tried, where and with what result turns scattered effort into knowledge you can build on.
cards.quote: I sent a man to South America to find what I want; he found it; but lost the place where he found it, so he might as well never have found it at all.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. A World-hunt for Filament Material ¶22
cards.apply_it: Start a running log for your current project today: date, what you tried, what happened.

quiz.question: Why did Edison say his South American explorer "might as well never have found it at all"?
options: The sample was damaged in transit
He lost the place where he found it
quiz.explanation: Without a record of the location, the discovery could not be used again.

cards.title: Try many variations, then pick the one that shows promise and build on it
cards.body:
Edison compared his chemical research to the plant breeder Luther Burbank, who would plant a whole acre, walk through it in bloom, and pick out the one plant with promise to breed from. Edison worked the same way. He would run hundreds or thousands of trials, follow up the one that pointed in the right direction, and drop the rest. For his storage battery he tested mixtures in steady steps, kept the best three proportions, then tested every quality of material within those.

You can use this for writing, design or marketing. Make many rough versions quickly, pick the strongest, and refine that one.
cards.quote: So, when I am after a chemical result that I have in mind, I may make hundreds or thousands of experiments out of which there may be one that promises results in the right direction.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶33
cards.apply_it: For something you are creating, make five quick rough versions instead of one careful one. Then pick the best and improve it.

quiz.question: Whose method did Edison compare his chemical experiments to?
quiz.explanation: Like Burbank choosing the best plant from an acre, Edison ran many trials and developed only the most promising.

cards.title: Experiment small before you build full size
cards.body:
Edison was happy to spend heavily on research overall, but he kept each single experiment as cheap as he could. He told an assistant that many inventors spend all their money by building things life-size at once, instead of first trying ideas freely on a small scale.

The same applies to a business idea, a new habit or a home project. A small, cheap test lets you make more attempts with the same budget and learn faster. Save the full-size version for after the small one has shown you what works.
cards.quote: A good many inventors try to develop things life-size, and thus spend all their money, instead of first experimenting more freely on a small scale.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶55
cards.apply_it: What is the smallest, cheapest version of your next idea you could test this week?

quiz.question: What mistake did Edison say many inventors make?
options: They build things life-size first and spend all their money
They work in teams that are too large
They rely too much on books
quiz.explanation: He advised experimenting freely on a small scale before committing money to full-size versions.

cards.title: Stop experimenting and you start going backward
cards.body:
Edison told the superintendent of his cement plant that the only way to stay ahead was to keep experimenting, because if you did not, a competitor would. When something went wrong, the answer was to experiment until you reached the bottom of the trouble. He was wary of over-standardising products, and said that as soon as an article was perfect, that was the time to start improving it.

In any field, standing still is a quiet way of falling behind. Keeping one small experiment going in your work, a new method, tool or approach, keeps you learning while others coast.
cards.quote: The only way to keep ahead of the procession is to experiment. If you don't, the other fellow will.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶55
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine at work or home and run a small experiment to improve it this week.

quiz.question: According to Edison, what happens when you stop experimenting?
quiz.explanation: He believed that without experiment there is no progress, and a competitor will overtake you.

cards.title: When someone says there is only one way, look for forty-eight more
cards.body:
At the ore-milling works, an engineer brought Edison three sketches for a new machine. Edison rejected them. The engineer said there was simply no other way to do it. Edison asked whether he really meant those drawings were the only ways, and the engineer said yes. Edison said nothing more. On Monday he laid forty-eight other ways on the engineer's desk without a word. One of them, improved with ideas from others, was put into use.

"There's no other way" usually means "I have stopped looking". When you feel stuck, set yourself a number, ten or twenty alternatives, and keep going until you reach it.
cards.quote: Do you mean to say that these drawings represent the only way to do this work?
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶68
cards.apply_it: Take a problem you feel stuck on and list ten different ways to tackle it, including silly ones.

quiz.question: How did Edison respond when told there was no other way to do the job?
options: He accepted the engineer's best design
He returned with sketches of forty-eight other ways
quiz.explanation: Over a weekend he sketched forty-eight alternatives, and one of them was used.

cards.title: Let a hard problem make you curious, not discouraged
cards.body:
His staff noticed that a stubborn difficulty, one that looked impossible, actually cheered Edison up. It set him thinking, and soon he would write out a list of eliminations, additions and changes to try. Ideas poured out, and some that sounded ridiculous at first turned out to be the answer. His mathematician Francis Upton said the same: difficulties made him cheerful and started him thinking.

You cannot always choose how a problem lands, but you can choose your next move. Treat a hard obstacle as a puzzle and start listing ways to come at it from different sides. That shift alone often loosens the knot.
cards.quote: A good stiff difficulty--one which may, perhaps, appear to be an unsurmountable obstacle--only serves to make Edison cheerful, and brings out variations of his methods in experimenting.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶67
cards.apply_it: Write today's biggest obstacle at the top of a page, then list five different angles of attack beneath it.

quiz.question: How did a seemingly impossible obstacle usually affect Edison?
options: It made him delegate the problem
It made him abandon the project
It made him cheerful and full of new approaches
It made him angry with his staff
quiz.explanation: His associates saw difficulties start a stream of suggestions for attacking the problem from several sides.

cards.title: Sometimes the fix is simply to keep going for a few more hours
cards.body:
For an early lamp filament, Edison found that a crumbly mix of lampblack and tar turned into a smooth, workable putty if kneaded long enough. An assistant told him something was wrong, because it still crumbled after more than an hour. Edison asked how long he had kneaded it and told him to keep going for a few hours more. After prolonged kneading the mass did change, and filaments from it were used in early successful lamps.

Some processes simply take longer than our patience. Before deciding a method is broken, check whether you have given it the time it needs.
cards.quote: Well, just keep on for a few hours more and it will come out all right
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶38
cards.apply_it: Is there a practice, recipe or skill you have judged too early? Give it one more honest, longer attempt.

quiz.question: What did Edison tell the assistant whose tar mixture kept crumbling?
options: Throw it away and start again
Keep kneading for a few hours more
quiz.explanation: The mixture only needed far longer kneading, and it then became a usable putty.

cards.title: Never settle for a fuzzy answer when you can break the problem into pieces
cards.body:
Edison would not accept doubtful results. If an experiment left an uncertainty, it was taken apart and checked until the answer was clear either way. When a sample of copper wire from a trusted supplier tested worse than before, he did not shrug it off as a bad batch. He asked for it to be cut into lengths and each one tested, to find out whether a single bad spot was to blame. His push for consistent copper helped set a quality standard for the electrical trade.

When a result puzzles you, split it up. Testing the parts separately often shows that one small fault explains the whole thing.
cards.quote: Perhaps the ---- wire had a bad spot in it. Please cut it up into lengths and test each one and send results to me immediately.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶70
cards.apply_it: Take a confusing result in your work, such as a bad month or a failing process, and break it into parts to examine one by one.

quiz.question: What did Edison ask for when a copper wire sample tested poorly?
options: The wire cut into lengths and each length tested
quiz.explanation: He wanted to know whether one bad spot explained the result, rather than accept an uncertain conclusion.

cards.title: Read across every field, including the light stuff, to know what is going on
cards.body:
At sixty-two Edison still read constantly. He said he read on astronomy, chemistry, biology, physics, music, mechanics, economics and more, took the journals of the scientific societies, and also read theatre and entertainment papers because he liked to know what was going on. Asked what kept him going, he said he did not live in the past but for today and tomorrow.

Ideas often come from the meeting of different fields. A broad, slightly unpredictable reading diet gives your mind more material to connect. Add one source a little outside your usual lane and see what it sparks.
cards.quote: I also read The Clipper, The Police Gazette, The Billboard, The Dramatic Mirror, and a lot of similar publications, for I like to know what is going on.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. The Social Side of Edison ¶31
cards.apply_it: Add one publication, podcast or newsletter from a field you know nothing about to your reading this week.

quiz.question: Why did Edison read popular entertainment papers alongside scientific journals?
options: He was planning to write for them
He liked to know what was going on
quiz.explanation: His wide reading, from science to popular papers, kept him informed about the whole world around him.

cards.title: Great work often comes from partners whose strengths fit together
cards.body:
Francis Upton described the heart of Menlo Park as three people. Edison poured out clear ideas, often sketched in three dimensions. John Kruesi, the Swiss superintendent, grasped the ideas and divided up the work so it got done fast and accurately. Charles Batchelor brought the patience and steady hands for delicate experiments, mounting tiny filaments for hours despite repeated failures.

The light bulb is often told as one man's story, but it took a team. Knowing what you are best at, and teaming up with people who cover your gaps, can multiply what you achieve alone.
cards.quote: It was an ideal combination, that of Edison, Batchelor, and Kruesi.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Memories of Menlo Park ¶13
cards.apply_it: Name one strength you bring to your team and one gap you have. Who could cover that gap?

quiz.question: What did John Kruesi contribute to the Menlo Park team?
options: Taking ideas and dividing the work so it was done quickly and accurately
quiz.explanation: Kruesi turned Edison's ideas into organised work, while Batchelor handled the finest experiments.

cards.title: Treat your team as colleagues and they will give you their best
cards.body:
Francis Jehl, one of the Menlo Park assistants, said the men around Edison trusted him and he trusted them. He never made them feel he was their employer in a hurtful way. He talked, argued and disagreed with them as an equal, and Jehl believed this was what made them so loyal and ready to do whatever he asked.

Titles and authority get compliance. Respect gets commitment. If you lead anyone, try arguing ideas on their merits rather than on rank, and see how much more people bring to the table.
cards.quote: He conversed, argued, and disputed with us all as if he were a colleague on the same footing.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Memories of Menlo Park ¶33
cards.apply_it: In your next team discussion, invite someone junior to challenge your idea, and genuinely weigh their point.

quiz.question: According to Francis Jehl, what made the Menlo Park staff so loyal to Edison?
options: He treated them as colleagues on an equal footing
quiz.explanation: Edison argued with them as an equal and never made them feel small, which earned deep loyalty.

cards.title: Your stamina is not everyone's: lead with other people's limits in mind
cards.body:
The Menlo Park team often worked through the night. Edison could sleep anywhere, almost at will, and seemed tireless. His long-time colleague Francis Upton admired him, but added a frank note: Edison never seemed to understand that other people's strength had limits, because his own seemed to have none. The book's authors also note that he sometimes used people up in pursuit of a goal.

If you are someone with lots of energy, this is worth remembering. What feels easy to you may be exhausting for others. Good teams last when the pace fits the people, not only the person at the front.
cards.quote: But I have often felt that Mr. Edison never could comprehend the limitations of the strength of other men, as his own physical and mental strength have always seemed to be without limit.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Memories of Menlo Park ¶16
cards.apply_it: Ask one teammate or family member this week whether the pace you set feels sustainable to them.

quiz.question: What criticism did Francis Upton offer of Edison?
options: He could not grasp the limits of other people's strength
quiz.explanation: Upton admired Edison but felt he never understood that others did not share his own seemingly limitless stamina.

cards.title: Pay for results, but protect people from losing out when they take a chance
cards.body:
When Edison wanted a workman to build something, he sketched it and wrote the price he would pay for the job on the sketch. If the workman's earnings at that price fell short, Edison still paid his regular wages. If he earned more than his wages, he kept the extra. The sketch marked $18 that John Kruesi received became the first phonograph.

It is a neat design for motivation: a clear target, an upside for speed and skill, and a safety net so nobody is punished for trying. You can apply the idea to bonuses, freelance work or even chores at home.
cards.quote: If the workman lost, I would pay his regular wages; if he made more than the wages, he kept it.
cards.locator: Chapter X. The Phonograph ¶6
cards.apply_it: Think of one task you hand to others. How could you reward a great result without punishing an honest miss?

quiz.question: What happened under Edison's piece-work deal if the job paid less than a workman's wages?
options: Edison still paid his regular wages
quiz.explanation: Workers kept any extra earnings but never fell below their normal wage.

cards.title: Hire people by watching them do the work
cards.body:
Edison's job interviews were practical. When J. H. Vail asked to run the dynamo room, Edison pointed to a heap of junk and told him to put it together and report when it was running. Vail did not even know what it was, learned a great deal finding out, got it running, and got the job. John Ott, asked if he could make a machine work, said yes, and that Edison need not pay him if he could not. Two weeks later Ott was running the shop.

A real task shows more than a polished interview. Whether you are hiring, choosing a partner or picking a contractor, ask to see a small piece of genuine work.
cards.quote: Put that together and let me know when it's running.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶43
cards.apply_it: Next time you choose someone to work with, set a short, real task and judge them on how they handle it.

quiz.question: How did J. H. Vail win the job of running the dynamo room?
options: He was recommended by a friend
He assembled a pile of parts into a working dynamo
quiz.explanation: Edison gave him a practical challenge, and doing it proved he could handle the job.

cards.title: Train people by breaking things and having them fix it again and again
cards.body:
When Edison needed twenty experts to install his telephones in England, he set up ten instruments around the laboratory and sabotaged them in every way he could think of: cut wires, short circuits, wrecked adjustments, dirt between the contacts. Each trainee was sent to find the fault. Only someone who found the trouble ten times in a row, in five minutes each time, was sent to London. About sixty men were tested to find twenty.

That is a clear standard and plenty of realistic practice. To build real skill in yourself or others, practise on real faults and set a bar for consistency, not one lucky success.
cards.quote: When he could find the trouble ten consecutive times, using five minutes each, he was sent to London.
cards.locator: Chapter IX. The Telephone, Motograph, and Microphone ¶18
cards.apply_it: For a skill you are building, set a consistency target, such as getting it right five times in a row, and practise until you reach it.

quiz.question: What standard did trainees have to meet before going to London?
options: Find the fault ten consecutive times, in five minutes each
Work a full year at Menlo Park
quiz.explanation: Only those who could reliably diagnose deliberate faults, ten times running, were sent.

cards.title: When experts call something impossible, let it sharpen your thinking
cards.body:
When Edison began work on the electric light in 1877, leading electricians had concluded that dividing electric current among many small lamps could not be done. One eminent English engineer called it a will-o'-the-wisp. The authors say such opinions only spurred Edison on once he had thought deeply and was convinced it could work. On 21 October 1879 a carbonised cotton thread in a glass bulb with almost no air glowed for over forty hours.

Expert doubt is worth taking seriously, and it often helps to understand exactly why they think it cannot be done. But "impossible" is sometimes just "nobody has found the way yet".
cards.quote: Opinions of this nature have ever been but a stimulus to Edison when he has given deep thought to a subject, and has become impressed with strong convictions of possibility
cards.locator: Chapter XI. The Invention of the Incandescent Lamp ¶8
cards.apply_it: Write down one thing in your field people say cannot be done. List the specific reasons they give, and which one you could test.

quiz.question: What did a carbonised cotton thread achieve in October 1879?
options: It glowed in a vacuum bulb for over forty hours
quiz.explanation: That forty-hour lamp proved the practical incandescent lamp was possible, despite expert doubts.

cards.title: Before you challenge an industry, learn it better than its insiders
cards.body:
Edison's goal for electric light was to copy everything gas lighting did, then do it better. So he studied gas in depth: costs, investment, how consumption rose and fell through the year, the fumes it gave off indoors, how it was sold. His notebooks set out a soft light with the mildness of gas, not a blinding one, and a whole distribution system like gas mains. An expert gas engineer later said Edison knew more about gas than anyone he had met.

The authors credit that preparation for the speed of what followed. If you hope to replace an existing product or habit, first understand why people use it.
cards.quote: Luther Stieringer, an expert gas engineer and inventor, whose services were early enlisted, once said that Edison knew more about gas than any other man he had ever met.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. The Invention of the Incandescent Lamp ¶43
cards.apply_it: Pick the main alternative to what you offer. Write down five reasons people choose it today.

quiz.question: How did Edison prepare to compete with gas lighting?
options: He ignored gas and focused on street lights
He studied gas so thoroughly that an expert said he knew more about it than anyone
quiz.explanation: His deep study of the gas business shaped what his electric system needed to do.

cards.title: If the pieces you need don't exist, be ready to make them yourself
cards.body:
A lamp alone could not light a city. Edison needed dynamos, switchboards, meters, sockets, fuses, underground cables, junction boxes and much more, and none of it existed or could be ordered. So he started a lamp factory at Menlo Park and trained men, boys and girls in an entirely new trade. Other shops were set up for dynamos, cables and fittings.

New ideas often need an ecosystem around them. Before launching, map every piece your idea depends on, from tools to skills to suppliers, and work out which ones you will have to build or teach yourself.
cards.quote: Now, not one of these miscellaneous things was in existence; not an outsider was sufficiently informed about such devices to make them on order, except perhaps the special wire.
cards.locator: Chapter XV. Introduction of the Edison Electric Light ¶9
cards.apply_it: List every piece your next project depends on. Circle any that do not exist yet or that no one around you can provide.

quiz.question: Why did Edison start his own factories for the lighting system?
options: Because almost none of the parts existed and nobody could make them to order
quiz.explanation: Every device in the new system was novel, so he had to set up production himself.

cards.title: When something finally works, go looking for what will break it
cards.body:
When Edison was told a new device was working well from every angle, his familiar response was to cheerfully send the team off to hunt for bugs. Before the first central station in New York opened for regular service, he and a few assistants spent weeks running tests meant to break the plant if they could, so they could prevent problems before customers met them. Later, testing his storage batteries in cars, he accused drivers of picking easy roads if nothing broke for several days.

Success is the best time to stress-test. Try to break your own work before your customers, readers or clients do it for you.
cards.quote: Well, boys, now let's find the bugs
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. The First Edison Central Station ¶21
cards.apply_it: Take something you have just finished and spend 15 minutes trying to break it or poke holes in it.

quiz.question: What did Edison say when told a new device worked perfectly?
quiz.explanation: He treated success as the signal to start hunting for weaknesses.

cards.title: Learn the work from the ground up, even when you are the boss
cards.body:
In 1881, while applying for eighty-nine patents, Edison personally supervised the laying of underground cables for his first New York lighting district. The authors say he did not just give orders. He worked in the trenches with the labourers, among the paving stones and traffic, helping lay tubes and fill junction boxes, because he wanted to know for himself how things went and what could be improved.

He also worked punishing hours and slept on piles of pipes, which nobody needs to copy. The useful part is being close to the real work. Leaders who see the details first-hand spot problems and improvements that reports miss.
cards.quote: Day and night he actually worked in the trenches with the laborers, amid the dirt and paving-stones and hurry-burly of traffic, helping to lay the tubes, filling up junction-boxes, and taking part in all the infinite detail.
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. The First Edison Central Station ¶17
cards.apply_it: Spend an hour this week doing or closely watching the front-line work your role depends on.

quiz.question: Why did Edison work in the trenches laying cables himself?
options: He wanted to see for himself how things went and what could be improved
It was required by the city
quiz.explanation: He wanted first-hand knowledge of the work so he could improve materials and methods.

cards.title: Earn customers' trust before you ask them to pay
cards.body:
When the Pearl Street station began supplying electric light in September 1882, Edison gave customers the light free for the first three months. He was confident in his system and his meters, but knew a brand-new plant might hit unexpected stoppages, and that early hiccups could make the public distrust the new light. Only once it had run smoothly did billing begin. Later, when J. P. Morgan doubted the meter, Edison suggested a strict test to settle it.

When you offer something new, think about what a buyer has to believe before paying. A trial period that lets you fix teething problems can protect your reputation.
cards.quote: During the first three months of operating the Pearl Street station light was supplied to customers without charge.
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. The First Edison Central Station ¶32
cards.apply_it: If you offer something new, design a low-risk way for the first customers to try it while you iron out problems.

quiz.question: How did Edison launch the Pearl Street electric service?
options: With a big discount for the first year
By charging a high price to signal quality
By supplying light free for the first three months
quiz.explanation: Free service gave him time to fix problems and build public confidence before billing began.

cards.title: After a public flop, decide quickly and change direction
cards.body:
In spring 1879 Edison showed his backers a row of platinum-wire lamps. One by one they flared and burnt out, leaving the machine shop in darkness. The investors went home unimpressed. That night Edison sat alone thinking. His assistant Francis Jehl recalled that in an emergency Edison always decided quickly and correctly what to do. The platinum lamps were packed away and the team turned to carbon, which led to the working lamp that October.

A setback in front of others stings. But it can also be useful information. Give yourself time to think, then make a clear decision and act on it, rather than defending the old plan.
cards.quote: After that exhibition we had a house-cleaning at the laboratory, and the metallic-filament lamps were stored away, while preparations were made for our experiments on carbon lamps.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Memories of Menlo Park ¶25
cards.apply_it: Think of a plan that has publicly stumbled. Set a date to decide clearly whether to fix it or switch course.

quiz.question: What did Edison do after the platinum lamps failed in front of his backers?
options: He kept improving platinum for years
He gave up on electric light
He put the platinum lamps away and turned to carbon
quiz.explanation: He decided the metal path was wrong and redirected the work to carbon filaments.

cards.title: When a venture fails, pay what you owe and reuse what you learned
cards.body:
Edison spent over two million dollars and years of work on a plant to extract iron from low-grade rock. The process worked, but iron prices collapsed and vast cheap ore was found in Minnesota. The plant had to close, heavily in debt. On the train home Edison told Walter Mallory that no company of his had ever failed to pay its debts. They would use what they had learned in some practical way. The crushing know-how went into a Portland cement business, and Edison started on a new storage battery. Within about three years the debts were paid in full.

A failed project still leaves you with skills, contacts and knowledge. Ask where they can be used next.
cards.quote: inasmuch as we had the knowledge gained from our experience in the concentrating problem, we must, if possible, apply it to some practical use
cards.locator: Results of Working Briquettes at the Crane Furnace ¶15
cards.apply_it: List three skills or insights you gained from a project that did not work out, and one place you could use each.

quiz.question: What did Edison do after closing the ore-milling plant?
options: He paid the debts in full and applied the knowledge to a cement business
He sold the patents and retired
quiz.explanation: He insisted on paying creditors and reused the crushing know-how in cement, alongside new battery work.

cards.title: Knowing your modest fallback frees you to take bold risks
cards.body:
When the ore-milling business failed and his fortune was gone, Edison worried about his creditors, but Mallory heard him mention his own loss only once. He said that personally he could always get a job as a telegrapher at $75 a month, and that would cover everything he needed.

It is a calm way to face loss. Knowing the floor beneath you, the simple life you could fall back on and still be fine, can shrink fear and make you braver. Many people find it helps to work out their own minimum honestly, so a setback looks survivable rather than catastrophic.
cards.quote: As far as I am concerned, I can any time get a job at $75 per month as a telegrapher, and that will amply take care of all my personal requirements.
cards.locator: Results of Working Briquettes at the Crane Furnace ¶16
cards.apply_it: Write down your own simple fallback: the modest work and lifestyle you could live with if a big bet failed.

quiz.question: How did Edison talk about his personal financial loss from the ore-milling venture?
options: He said he could always earn enough as a telegrapher at $75 a month
He refused to discuss it ever again
quiz.explanation: He saw his basic needs as easily covered, which let him focus on paying creditors and moving on.

cards.title: Feel a setback for a few days, then turn back to the future
cards.body:
Asked about past events in 1909, Edison said spilt milk did not interest him. He admitted he had spilt plenty, and that he felt it for a few days each time. But he soon forgot it and turned again to the future. Years later he visited his abandoned ore-milling plant, by then decaying, and said only that he had never felt better than in his years there, and that what they learned would benefit someone someday.

Note that he did not pretend losses did not hurt. He allowed a few days, then moved on. Giving yourself a short, honest window to feel a setback, then a clear point to look forward again, is a healthy pattern.
cards.quote: Spilt milk doesn't interest me. I have spilt lots of it, and while I have always felt it for a few days, it is quickly forgotten, and I turn again to the future.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. The Social Side of Edison ¶31
cards.apply_it: For a recent disappointment, decide on a date by which you will stop replaying it and plan one next step.

quiz.question: How did Edison describe his reaction to past mistakes?
options: He never felt them at all
He kept a list to review each year
He felt them for a few days, then turned to the future
quiz.explanation: He acknowledged the sting but did not let it hold him back for long.

cards.title: Halt a product that falls short, even when stopping is costly
cards.body:
Edison's first nickel-iron storage battery sold well, but reports showed that now and then a cell fell short of its rated capacity. He traced the main cause to the graphite inside. Shutting the factory meant a heavy loss and looked like failure. Carrying on meant more faulty batteries in circulation, and in the end a permanent failure. He stopped production and went back to the laboratory. It took about five more years of experiments, and the improved battery was better than anyone had expected.

Shipping something you know is flawed borrows against your reputation. Sometimes pausing is the braver and wiser choice.
cards.quote: He was not satisfied that the battery was a complete success, so he shut down and went to experimenting once more.
cards.locator: Chapter XXII. The Development of the Edison Storage Battery ¶26
cards.apply_it: Is there something you are delivering that you know is not good enough? Decide what you would need to fix before continuing.

quiz.question: Why did Edison stop making his first storage battery?
options: A rival had a better battery
Some cells fell short in capacity, and he would not keep selling a flawed product
quiz.explanation: He chose a costly pause and years of further work over selling batteries he knew had a weakness.

cards.title: Start each day open-minded, leaving yesterday's disappointments behind
cards.body:
When asked the secret of success, Edison always answered: hard work, based on hard thinking. The authors add that he had a happy knack of starting each day as open-minded as a child, putting aside the previous day's failures in favour of what tomorrow might bring. When he decided to build a better battery, he said he did not believe nature would hide the secret from a real, earnest hunt, and that he was going hunting.

Long projects wear people down when yesterday's frustrations pile up. A deliberate fresh start each morning, a short reset before you begin, can keep your thinking flexible.
cards.quote: Edison has the happy faculty of beginning the day as open-minded as a child--yesterday's disappointments and failures discarded and discounted by the alluring possibilities of to-morrow.
cards.locator: Chapter XXII. The Development of the Edison Storage Battery ¶6
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow morning, before starting work, write one line on what could go right today, and leave yesterday's setbacks off the page.

quiz.question: What did Edison say when asked the secret of achievement?
options: Hard work, based on hard thinking
quiz.explanation: He paired effort with thought, and the authors note he began each day free of yesterday's disappointments.

cards.title: Set an ambitious target, then keep iterating until you reach it
cards.body:
For his cement plant Edison designed a kiln 150 feet long, far bigger than the 60-foot kilns in use, and predicted it would turn out a thousand barrels a day. Rival makers laughed. The first run produced about four hundred. Edison's reply to the report was blunt: "Rotten. Try it again." The team learned the kiln step by step: 550, 750, 850, then 1,000 and finally over 1,100 barrels a day. Others in the industry soon adopted the design.

A bold target gives a team something to reach for, and steady iteration closes the gap. Keep refining rather than lowering the bar at the first disappointing result.
cards.quote: he was just as confident as ever that the kiln would make one thousand barrels per day
cards.locator: Chapter XX. Edison Portland Cement ¶15
cards.apply_it: Set one stretch target for a current project. Plan three small improvements to try before you consider lowering it.

quiz.question: What did Edison's long cement kiln eventually achieve?
quiz.explanation: Starting at about 400, the team iterated until the kiln beat Edison's target of 1,000 barrels a day.

cards.title: Guard your focus, even from honours and important visitors
cards.body:
When one of the great English universities offered Edison an honorary degree, he was deep in storage battery experiments and would not leave the work for a week or two. Friends urged him to go. He let the honour pass. Once, a dignitary in top hat and frock coat arrived with a gold medal at the very moment of an important experiment, and Edison refused to be interrupted. He kept his medals in a jumble at home.

You do not have to turn down every honour. But the habit is worth noticing: real work in progress came first. Decide in advance which interruptions are worth breaking deep focus for, and protect the rest.
cards.quote: Before him was something real--work to be accomplished--a problem to be solved.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. The Social Side of Edison ¶45
cards.apply_it: Block one 90-minute session this week where nothing short of an emergency may interrupt you.

quiz.question: Why did Edison turn down a trip to receive an honorary degree?
options: He was too ill to travel
He was deep in storage battery experiments and would not leave the work
quiz.explanation: He put the problem in front of him ahead of the honour, a striking example of guarding focus.

cards.title: Argue hard for your view, then admit it when the other side is right
cards.body:
Edison argued with great energy, pounding the table and piling up examples, and his deafness made it hard for others to get a word in. Some visitors left thinking he dismissed every opposing view. The authors say that was wrong. If the other person persisted until he had seen both sides, he would frankly admit his own view might be unsound and theirs right. After one loud argument he told his opponent his position had been completely rotten.

Strong opinions are fine if they are held loosely. Make your case fully, then listen fully, and be ready to say out loud that you were wrong.
cards.quote: I see now that my position was absolutely rotten.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIX. The Social Side of Edison ¶51
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, summarise the other person's argument back to them before replying.

quiz.question: What did Edison do once he had truly heard both sides of an argument?
options: Frankly admitted when his own position was wrong
quiz.explanation: Though forceful in debate, he admitted error openly once he understood the other side.

cards.title: Commit publicly to raise the stakes and give yourself a reason to deliver
cards.body:
Francis Upton, who worked closely with Edison for years, believed that Edison sometimes put himself in a tight spot on purpose, for example by announcing results before they were ready, so that he would have every reason to get himself out of it. Difficulties, Upton said, made Edison cheerful and started a stream of ideas that did not stop until the problem was solved.

Used with care, public commitment can be a powerful motivator, though promising too early carries a real risk to your credibility. A modest version is to tell a friend or colleague what you will deliver and by when.
cards.quote: I have often felt that Mr. Edison got himself purposely into trouble by premature publications and otherwise, so that he would have a full incentive to get himself out of the trouble.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Memories of Menlo Park ¶32
cards.apply_it: Tell one person what you will finish this week and when, then ask them to check in.

quiz.question: According to Francis Upton, why did Edison sometimes announce things early?
options: To give himself full incentive to solve the problem
quiz.explanation: Upton thought Edison created pressure on purpose to drive himself to find a solution.

cards.title: Keep old discoveries on file: one may solve tomorrow's crisis
cards.body:
Edison's telephone business in England was threatened by a claim that its receiver infringed Bell's patent. His representative cabled for help, and Edison told him to hold the fort. He reached back to a curious effect he had found years earlier: friction between a metal spring and moist chalk changed with electric current. From it he built a loud-speaking chalk receiver with no magnet at all. The English company soon merged with its rival on good terms.

Ideas that seem useless when you find them can become exactly what you need later. Keep a note of odd results, and revisit them when you are stuck.
cards.quote: the phenomenon discovered by me years previous, that the friction of a rubbing electrode passing over a moist chalk surface was varied by electricity.
cards.locator: Chapter IX. The Telephone, Motograph, and Microphone ¶17
cards.apply_it: Look through old notes or projects for one idea you set aside. Could it help with a problem you have now?

quiz.question: How did Edison get around the threatened patent problem in England?
options: He built a chalk receiver based on a discovery he had made years before
He moved the business to France
quiz.explanation: He drew on an old, unused observation about chalk and friction to invent a different receiver.

cards.title: Open your books, and people will trust you when the cash is short
cards.body:
At his Schenectady works Edison had huge orders but no money, and needed $200,000 of copper. He and Samuel Insull went to the copper company and explained exactly where they stood. The owner asked if his bookkeeper could look at their books. They said come right up. The bookkeeper found the orders were real, and for years the company let Edison have all the copper he needed on credit.

Honesty about a tight spot, backed by open records, can win you more support than a confident front. If you need help from a supplier, lender or partner, show them the facts.
cards.quote: He said: 'I will see what I can do. Will you let my bookkeeper look at your books?' We said: 'Come right up and look them over.'
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI. Edison in Commerce and Manufacture ¶10
cards.apply_it: If you need flexibility from someone, prepare a clear, honest summary of your situation to show them.

quiz.question: How did Edison get $200,000 of copper with no cash?
options: He borrowed from J. P. Morgan
He promised a patent in return
He let the supplier's bookkeeper inspect his books, which showed real orders
quiz.explanation: Open books proved the business was sound, and the supplier extended credit for years.

cards.title: Put agreements in writing, even with people you trust
cards.body:
Edison was generous but often careless in business. He once put $800 into a small repair shop for two former workers, in return for half the profits. Years later he asked to sell his share. They told him he owned nothing, because he had no papers to prove it. Other handshake deals and loosely worded contracts cost him his share of European lighting profits.

Good will is no substitute for a clear record. Even a short email setting out who puts in what and who gets what can save a friendship, and a lot of money, later.
cards.quote: You don't own this machinery. This is our machinery. You have no papers to show anything. You had better get out.
cards.locator: Chapter XXVI. Edison in Commerce and Manufacture ¶8
cards.apply_it: Is there an informal deal in your life, a loan or shared project, that would benefit from a short written note? Write it this week.

quiz.question: What happened to Edison's $800 investment in his former workers' shop?
options: He lost it because he had no papers proving his share
quiz.explanation: Without written proof of ownership, the partners simply denied he had any stake.

cards.title: Let experiment, not received theory, have the final word
cards.body:
A long-time assistant said Edison was never held back by theory, and tested ideas for proof. When he proposed pouring a whole concrete house in one go, experts said it could not work, because the stones would sink in the wet cement. His experiments showed otherwise. Earlier, when textbook opinion held that a dynamo's internal resistance should match its external load, he built one the opposite way and reached about 90 per cent efficiency, against roughly 40 per cent for the best machines then in use.

Theory is a useful guide but a poor final judge. When a claim matters and can be tested, test it.
cards.quote: He is never hindered by theory, but resorts to actual experiment for proof.
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶15
cards.apply_it: Find one "rule" in your work that everyone accepts. Design a small test to see whether it actually holds for you.

quiz.question: How did Edison respond to experts who said a poured concrete house was impossible?
options: He agreed and dropped the idea
He ran experiments that showed it could be done
He hired the experts to redesign it
quiz.explanation: He relied on experiment over theory, and the tests proved the doubters wrong.

cards.title: A path others have given up on may need only one unexpected change
cards.body:
One of Edison's experienced staff spent a long time trying to make a chemical compound with certain properties and only half succeeded. Edison was sure it could be done and tried it himself. He followed the very same route, but made one change nobody had imagined in one step of the process, and produced a compound that nearly met his specification. The assistant said it was not the only time he had seen this happen.

When something "has been tried", it is worth asking which steps were taken for granted. Changing a single assumption on a well-worn route can open it up again.
cards.quote: Edison can travel along a well-used road and still find virgin soil
cards.locator: Chapter XXIV. Edison's Method in Inventing ¶14
cards.apply_it: Choose a problem you or others have "already tried". List each step and question one that everyone took for granted.

quiz.question: How did Edison succeed where his assistant had only partly succeeded?
options: He followed the same path but changed one operation in an unexpected way
He used a completely new method
He bought the compound from a supplier
quiz.explanation: A single unexpected change to one step on a familiar route made the difference.
